Present Perfect Passive to Report Events
You use the passive form of the Present Perfect tense when the action is not done by the subject but rather to the subject. Often, it is not known who has done the action.
In articles, stories and academic writing, you often use the passive form of the Present Perfect tense. This gives your writing a more sophisticated and dynamic quality.
Look at the following examples of an active and passive sentence. Compare their structures.

Active:
Experts have dated prehistoric cave paintings as being done between 40,000 BC and 10,000 BC.

Passive:
Prehistoric cave paintings have been dated by experts as being done between 40,000 BC and 10,000 BC.

As you can see, the structure of the Present Perfect passive is:

Subject + has/have been + past participle
The cave paintings have been cited as the earliest known art.
Through the cave paintings we have been given an insight into the lifestyle of primitive humans.
Animals have been painted on all of the walls in these caves.
The animal images in the caves have been done in mainly red and black.
Present Perfect to Talk About Past Experiences
You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experiences. When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.
For example:

I have learned English. = I learned English in the past and now I can speak English.
He has bought a painting. = He bought the painting in the past and now he has a painting.
When you want to refer to an action that recently happened, you use the word just.

For example:
I have just started the car.
When you want to emphasize that an action started and is ongoing at the present time, you use the word already.

For example:
I have already started the car.
When you ask questions using the Present Perfect, you often use words like ever and yet.

For example:
Have these types of discoveries ever come to light any way but by accident?

You use never in negative statements.

For example:
I have never been into a prehistoric cave, but I have wanted to visit one.
I have read several accounts of how someone had just come across an opening and wandered in to find 35,000-year-old pictures.
They have already been documented in France, Spain, Romania and Sulawesi.

images.text: I have never been into a prehistoric cave, but I have wanted to visit one. Have these types of discoveries ever come to light any way but by accident? Probably not.</br></br>I have read several accounts of how someone has just come across an opening and wandered in to find 35,000-year-old pictures. They have already been documented in France, Spain, Romania and Sulawasi. Many in Africa have not been fully explored yet.

The cave paintings have been cited as the earliest known art. They have been dated by experts as  being done between 40,000 BC and 10,000 BC, during the Old Stone Age period.
Through the cave paintings we have been given an insight into the lifestyle of primitive humans.
</br></br>
Animals have been painted on all of the walls in these caves. The obvious importance of animals in the lives of early man can be seen from this. However, the depictions have given us a far better understanding.
</br></br>
The images are considered to be milestones in the advancement of early man's mental facilities. Furthermore, the artists needed high level manual dexterity. Man was beginning to develop intellectually and master skills that allowed him to show his creativity.

The animal images in the caves have been done in mainly red and black.  Although many animals pictured on the walls were hunted by the primitive man, others were not. So they cannot all be tied to hunting ritual.
</br></br>
Also scattered throughout the caves are stenciled red ochre hand prints. What is most interesting is the fact that even though these artists clearly had the capacity to depict humans, they chose not to.
